ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

Bronchial asthma: 5

A patient undergoing specialist investigation develops an excessive fall in expiratory airflow during a bronchial challenge test. The result is interpreted alongside the clinical history. Which physiological property of the airways is being demonstrated by this response?

  1. Variable expiratory airflow limitation
  2. Repeat objective testing when symptomatic or use an appropriate variability test
  3. Type 2 airway inflammation
  4. Trigger-associated worsening of airway narrowing
  5. Bronchial hyperresponsiveness
Answer and explanation

Bronchial hyperresponsiveness

Excessive airway narrowing to a stimulus is characteristic of hyperresponsive airways, although challenge results require clinical interpretation.

Option explanations

Bronchial hyperresponsiveness: Excessive airway narrowing to a stimulus is characteristic of hyperresponsive airways, although challenge results require clinical interpretation.

Variable expiratory airflow limitation: Episodic symptoms plus demonstrably variable expiratory airflow support asthma; variability is a defining diagnostic feature. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Repeat objective testing when symptomatic or use an appropriate variability test: Normal spirometry between episodes does not exclude asthma; diagnostic confirmation may require repeated or alternative testing. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Type 2 airway inflammation: Eosinophilic inflammation is a common asthma phenotype, involving pathways such as IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13; not all asthma is eosinophilic. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Trigger-associated worsening of airway narrowing: Viral infections, allergens and irritants can provoke symptoms in susceptible airways without each episode implying bacterial pneumonia. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
